en: The Rise of Kerala:
*Svapnamañjarī*, Canto One.
In ancient times, that descendant of Bhṛgu, the enemy of his enemies and disciple of Purāri,
dwelt in a leaf-hut on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains through the power of his asceticism.
The axe, generally kept idle, lay far away in a corner;
the sage beheld it lying there in concealment, as if it were the very pride of its former self.
Even if he is unarmed, a cruel sage who deprives living beings of their lives is indeed a source of terror to the world; for a serpent, though devoid of fangs, is still dangerous. (3)
Although the descendant of Bhṛgu was endowed with spiritual accomplishments and possessed unbroken valor in his conduct,
he was nonetheless tormented by some unseen, subtle, and sharp-edged affliction.
Yet no expansion occurred within that inert self,
just as there is no sound from the strike of a hand upon a bronze vessel filled with water.
Then, on one occasion, having obtained permission and with his axe as his sole companion, Rāma made this request in a voice choked by tears and sighs: (6)
O Lord, I am unable to carry this woman who causes such great distress; she is like a stone tied around one's neck that leads only to total ruin.
The wind, intent solely on the effort of carrying away [my fragrance], always passes by the door of my hermitage without even touching it. (8)
O Creator, when singing has begun and the connection [of notes] is established,
the arrows remain suddenly motionless like statues, with their throats choked.
Setting aside his Vedic studies and smiling gently, the Blessed One,
who was skilled in speech, spoke these words rich in the truth of creation:
"May it be well with you, O hero of ever-dauntless deeds!"
Why has this desire for happiness arisen in you unexpectedly on the path of latent tendencies? (28) My dear, all human beings indeed seek to acquire their own self-interest;
nevertheless, from its very root, the world finds the locus of its happiness dependent upon others. (29)
You are constantly pursued by a harsh desert whirlwind of the singular sin of slaughtering your brother— a wind whose very nature is fear and dreams—
and by those who roar like demons, utterly devoid of the wealth of affection.
"You have become the personification of the prowess of those who live by the sword.
O dear one, at Syamantapañcaka, the ancestors led by Bhṛgu were satiated;
I believe their throats have been scorched by the hot water of your pride. (31-32)

O Hero, you have indeed uprooted the thorn that was a thorn to the field; yet you have not sown in its place the seed that produces a succession of happiness. By you, who sport like a forest fire, [the enemy] has been destroyed.
O Rāma, you have uprooted this dense forest together with its poisonous creepers and its multitude of great medicinal herbs; along with it,
even the shade that provides solace to the world has been utterly destroyed.

Just as one whose hands are the kinsman of the universe does not enter the blind well of worldly existence— which is steeped in darkness— so too, because your soul is covered by sin, the world’s stainless affection does not enter it.
Furthermore, the succession of the fruits of actions neither perishes nor is it lost.
For an injury that is not met with a counter-injury, my son, is not seen as such. O son,
destiny— whether sown in the past, performed in the present, or hidden—
is never rendered fruitless.
O dear one, a subtle-bodied sense of sinfulness dwells within the hearts of men;
through its connection, even a gentle breeze may become like a buffalo.
A living being is seized by enemies, yet it is never truly created anywhere.
Therefore, the wise man should not harm another; this is the eternal dharma.
In the *vākas*, *anuvākas*, *niṣads*, and *upaniṣads*, this fourfold auspicious tradition has been declared both in detail and in brief.
In my creation, all beings indeed possess the right to live.
This is a path that leads astray, by which even a powerful man is as if devoured while rendered helpless.
O Rāma, virtues are as fleeting as the flower of the Śigru tree; they are fragile by their very nature.
A self-possessed man should not tread upon these like a beast.
(43) A person comes alone and departs alone, subject to his own power;
life spent for one's own sake is in vain, but it is meaningful when dedicated to the sake of others. (44)
The wise person should not wait for absolute happiness within cyclic existence;
for even though there are distinctions of caste, the shadow of every entity is indeed time itself.
While the entire world is intent solely on wandering, distinguished by place and time, [it remains subject to this].
The life of a living being is afflicted by death at every moment and is unreal;
nevertheless, it persists, producing a continuity of merit for the soul.
This self-satisfaction, rooted in the satisfaction of the world, is most weighty.
Liberation is not some exalted state to be achieved through the restraints (yamas) and other practices;
rather, my son, it is simply the seasonal course of life in which one’s existence flourishes.
[This is known] by those who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedic scriptures, and who are perfected in their vows and rituals.
The Dharma, characterized by the welfare and happiness of others, is not realized [by mere silence].
O dear one, when Truth remains established in silence, Dharma remains awake without effort; but when that Truth is made talkative by the implication of its meaning, Dharma merely sleeps. 49–50.
For even in this transformed cycle of existence, that which has truth as its essence is not subverted;
indeed, even when reflected in water, a tree does not become upside down.
Water always flows toward the lower surface, and smoke always rises upward.
There is indeed a fixed order, however subtle, in the sequence of the universe's activities.
This question concerning the connection between life and its purpose is exceedingly ancient;
it is thus beyond answer, O friend—do not fall into delusion.
Even if not reached and even if far away, it is clearly seen like the horizon;
therefore, this great mirror of humanity is by no means useless.
It is bound together by both loose and firm accumulations of effort.
The progress of mortals is seen to be like a staircase of wheels, fraught with affliction.
First, the weapon strikes the compassionate one who bears joy;
thereafter the enemy, then the friend, and finally one's own kinsman.
For victory gained through violence is seen as defeat,
while even defeat, when cherished with affection, is victory. He who seeks to win over the world performs a "red-dyeing" (raktarañjanā) [of his own character].
Though he be wise and a hero, he is not truly confident like a seasoned man;
for a son is not cleansed by the repayment of an injury.
A knot becomes even harder when it is tied again with a thread.
A victorious man may acquire wealth, revile others, and cut through everything;
yet even against the fierce and violent God of Death (Kṛtānta), he cannot prevail. Furthermore, pride in one's own prowess is not appropriate for you who seek liberation.

Oil is beneficial for the body, yet it leaves a stain upon the mirror. (61) Therefore, let this sinful practice, which is like a battle-axe, be abandoned from afar today—by which even your learning, as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, is being crushed. (62)
O Nandana, by its mere presence, the axe transforms the mortal;
the mind, delighted by the practice, assumes the pride of accomplishment.
"This is that very axe which must be abandoned"—thus speaks the arrogant boaster with bold words.
"May this [speech] of yours, acting as a physician for your manly prowess, be effective for your benefit.
Having heard these words of Viriñca, whose syllables promised liberation from the curse, Rāma turned back, as if bearing a new birth.
